    Goal

    Audit the software on a real computer. Then use the Linux command line to set up the folders for an invented small office (Harbour Street Physio), search its server log for problems, and lock down its private files.

    Work in the worksheet. Save your copy as week3_lab.md. Any text editor works, or you can copy it into Word or Google Docs and save it as a PDF.

    Callout

    Privacy. In Part 1, do not record user names, device names or anything you would not want your tutor to see. The kind of software is enough; you do not need version numbers.

    Part 1: software audit (about 30 minutes)

    Use “See the software on your computer” in Section 3.1.

    1. List five application programs on your computer, and say in a few words what each is for.
    2. List five pieces of system software:
      • the operating system and its version
      • at least two utilities (for example antivirus, backup, firewall, updater)
      • any others you can find (for example a driver)
      Say in a few words what each one does.
    3. Look at Windows Update or Software Update. Is the operating system up to date? Write yes, no or “can’t tell”, and one sentence on why updates matter.

    Part 2: command-line lab (about 60 minutes)

    Before you start:

    • JSLinux is wiped when the page reloads. Do the whole lab in one sitting, and copy your work into the worksheet before you close the tab.
    • If something goes wrong, you can always start again from step 1.

    Step 1: start Linux and load the log file

    1. Start JSLinux as in Section 3.3 (x86_64 Alpine Linux, Console).
    2. Load the office’s log file, lab_files/server.log, in one of two ways:
      • Upload (easiest): download server.log from the Files box above to your computer. In JSLinux, click the up arrow below the terminal and choose the file. It is copied to your home folder.
      • Paste: JSLinux can drop characters if you paste too much at once, so paste in two blocks. Copy block 1, right-click in the terminal and choose Paste, and wait for the prompt localhost:~# to come back. Then do the same with block 2. Press Enter if the prompt does not come back.

    Block 1 (creates the file with the first 10 lines):

    cat > server.log << 'END'
2026-11-02 08:01:12 INFO User olivia.thompson logged in
2026-11-02 08:03:40 ERROR Disk usage above 90 percent on /data
2026-11-02 08:15:05 WARNING Failed login for user admin
2026-11-02 08:15:09 WARNING Failed login for user admin
2026-11-02 08:15:14 WARNING Failed login for user admin
2026-11-02 08:20:31 INFO User jack.wilson logged in
2026-11-02 09:02:47 INFO Backup started
2026-11-02 09:44:18 ERROR Backup failed: storage device not found
2026-11-02 10:10:02 INFO User priya.nair logged in
2026-11-02 11:30:55 WARNING Failed login for user jack.wilson
END

    Block 2 (adds the last 10 lines; note the >>):

    cat >> server.log << 'END'
2026-11-02 11:31:20 INFO User jack.wilson logged in
2026-11-02 12:05:33 INFO Software update installed: printer driver 4.2
2026-11-02 13:47:09 ERROR Printer offline: OFFICE-PRN-01
2026-11-02 14:22:41 WARNING Failed login for user admin
2026-11-02 14:22:46 WARNING Failed login for user admin
2026-11-02 15:00:00 INFO Backup started
2026-11-02 15:38:12 INFO Backup completed
2026-11-02 16:59:58 INFO User olivia.thompson logged out
2026-11-02 17:04:23 ERROR Antivirus definitions out of date
2026-11-02 17:30:00 INFO User jack.wilson logged out
END
    1. Check it worked: ls should list server.log, and wc -l server.log should show 20 server.log. If it shows fewer lines, type rm server.log and load it again.

    Step 2: build the office folders

    Using commands only:

    1. Make a folder office with three folders inside it: finance, hr and public.
    2. Create two empty files in hr: staff_list.txt and leave_requests.txt.
    3. Create one empty file in finance: budget_2026.txt.
    4. Create public/notice.txt containing the line Office closed on 26 January. Use echo and >.
    5. Move server.log into the office folder.
    6. Go into office, and list everything with ls -R. The -R option lists the folders inside too.

    Step 3: copy, rename and delete

    1. Copy public/notice.txt into finance.
    2. Rename the copy in finance to notice_copy.txt.
    3. Delete finance/notice_copy.txt.
    4. Check with ls finance that only budget_2026.txt is left.

    Step 4: investigate the server log

    Run commands that answer these questions. Record each command and its answer in the worksheet.

    1. How many lines does the log have?
    2. Show only the ERROR lines.
    3. How many ERROR lines are there?
    4. How many failed logins were there? Search for Failed login.
    5. How many of those failed logins were for the user admin?
    6. Save all the ERROR lines into a new file called errors.txt, then show that file.

    Step 5: lock down the files

    1. Make both hr files readable and writable by their owner only.
    2. Make public/notice.txt readable by everyone but writable only by its owner.
    3. Show the result with ls -l hr public.
    4. Take one screenshot of the ls -l output.
      • Windows: press Windows + Shift + S.
      • macOS: press Cmd + Shift + 4.

    Step 6: save your command log

    1. Type history.
    2. Select the output with the mouse, right-click, choose Copy, and paste it into the worksheet.
    3. Next to each command, write one line on what it did. You may leave out typing mistakes.

    Part 3: what the log tells you (about 15 minutes)

    The office manager is not technical. In the worksheet, write three short points telling them what the log shows and what they should do. Think about: - the repeated failed logins for admin - the failed backup - the out-of-date antivirus

    Part 4: reflection (about 15 minutes, including tidying)

    Write 100 to 150 words:

    1. What did you find hardest about the command line, and what helped?
    2. Why did you set the HR files to owner-only? Use the words least privilege.
    3. Give one example of how a cyber security analyst or a data analyst could use grep at work.

    Check your work

    How it is marked

    Your tutor marks each criterion as meets, partly or not yet:

    Criterion What the tutor looks for
    Accurate Software is sorted correctly. The commands work and give the right answers. The permissions are right.
    Complete Every item on the checklist is done.
    Evidence The command log and the screenshot show the work was done in the terminal.
    Explanation The command notes, the manager points and the reflection are in your own words.

    Key Points

    • Each week has five blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge, Build and Quiz.
    • System software runs the computer; application software helps a person do a task.
    • Installing updates quickly is one of the best security habits.
    • The operating system manages the hardware, programs, files and users.
    • A path is the address of a file in the folder tree.
    • The command line is precise, repeatable and widely used in cyber security and data work.
    • Permissions control who can read, write and run each file.
    • Give every person and program only the access they need, and no more.
    • grep and permissions are everyday tools for analysts.

    Content from Week 4: Algorithms and programming basics

    Last updated on 2026-11-23 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What will I learn in Week 4, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    • What is an algorithm, and how do I design one?
    • What are the building blocks every program uses?
    • How do searching algorithms compare?
    • How does a CPU run a program, one instruction at a time?
    • How does a program in a language like Python reach the CPU?
    • Can I design and test an algorithm before any code is written?

    Objectives

    Week 4 overview

    What you will be able to do this week

    • Use variables, selection (IF), repetition (loops) and functions in an algorithm.
    • Check an algorithm by hand with a trace table, and compare linear and binary search.
    • Run a short machine-level program on a model CPU and watch it work.

    4.1 Problem solving and algorithms

    Time: about 35 minutes (25 minutes reading, 10 minutes exercises).

    What an algorithm is

    An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem. A recipe is an algorithm; so are the steps for resetting a password or working out someone’s pay.

    A good algorithm is:

    • clear: each step means only one thing;
    • ordered: the steps happen in a set order;
    • finite: it always finishes.

    Computers can only follow algorithms. They cannot guess what you meant. A program is an algorithm written in a programming language (such as Python) so a computer can run it. This week you will design algorithms without a programming language, using pseudocode and flowcharts. In Introduction to Programming you will turn ideas like these into Python.

    Computational thinking

    Computational thinking is a set of four habits for turning a messy problem into an algorithm.

    Habit What it means Example: planning a staff roster
    Decomposition Break the problem into smaller parts Collect availability; count shifts; assign people; check the rules; publish
    Pattern recognition Spot what repeats or is similar Every weekday needs the same shifts
    Abstraction Keep only the details that matter, and ignore the rest A person’s availability matters; their favourite colour does not
    Algorithm design Write the steps in order “For each shift, choose an available person with the fewest shifts so far”

    Data scientists use these habits to plan an analysis. Cyber security analysts use them to plan how to investigate an incident.

    Writing algorithms as pseudocode

    Pseudocode is structured plain English that looks a little like code. It has no strict rules, but this course uses the keywords below, written in capitals, so everyone’s pseudocode looks alike.

    Keyword What it does Example
    INPUT Get a value from the user INPUT hours
    OUTPUT Show a result OUTPUT "Total: ", total
    SET ... TO Store a value in a variable SET pay TO hours * rate
    IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... END IF Choose between two paths see below
    WHILE ... END WHILE Repeat while a condition is true see Section 4.2
    FOR EACH ... IN ... END FOR Repeat once for every item in a list see Section 4.2
    FUNCTION ... END FUNCTION, RETURN A named, reusable set of steps see Section 4.2

    Indent the steps inside an IF, a loop or a function, so the structure is easy to see.

    Example: a parking fee. Parking costs $3 an hour, with a daily maximum of $15.

    INPUT hours
SET fee TO hours * 3
IF fee > 15 THEN
    SET fee TO 15
END IF
OUTPUT "Fee: $", fee

    Drawing algorithms as flowcharts

    A flowchart shows the same algorithm as a diagram. Each kind of step has its own shape, and arrows show the order.

    Shape Name Used for
    Rounded rectangle (oval) Terminator Start and End
    Parallelogram Input / output INPUT and OUTPUT
    Rectangle Process Calculations and SET
    Diamond Decision A yes/no question; it has two arrows out, labelled Yes and No
    Arrow Flow line The order of the steps

    Here is the parking fee as a flowchart:

            ( Start )
            |
     / INPUT hours /
            |
  [ SET fee TO hours * 3 ]
            |
      < fee > 15 ? > --Yes--> [ SET fee TO 15 ]
            |                        |
            No                       |
            |<-----------------------+
     / OUTPUT fee /
            |
         ( End )

    Making flowcharts in diagrams.net. diagrams.net (https://app.diagrams.net/) is a free diagram tool that runs in your browser, with no account.

    1. Open it. A blank page appears. If you are asked where to save, choose Device or Decide later.
    2. Open the shapes panel, search for flowchart, and drag shapes onto the page.
    3. Double-click a shape to type in it.
    4. Hover over a shape and drag one of its small arrows to connect it to the next shape.
    5. To save a picture, use the menu: File > Export as > PNG. In the simple layout, the menu is under the ⋯ button.

    You can also draw flowcharts by hand and photograph them.

    Challenge

    Exercises

    About 10 minutes. Answers are at the end.

    1. Use decomposition to break “organise a team lunch” into four smaller steps.
    2. Which flowchart shape would you use for: (a) INPUT age; (b) “Is age 18 or over?”; (c) SET total TO total + price; (d) the end of the algorithm?
    3. Write pseudocode that asks for a temperature in Celsius and outputs “Hot” if it is over 30, and “Not hot” otherwise.

    1. For example: find out who is coming; choose a place that suits everyone’s diet; book a table; tell everyone the time and place.

      1. parallelogram (input/output); (b) diamond (decision); (c) rectangle (process); (d) rounded rectangle (terminator).

    3. For example:

      INPUT celsius
IF celsius > 30 THEN
    OUTPUT "Hot"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Not hot"
END IF

    4.2 The building blocks of programs

    Time: about 40 minutes (25 minutes reading, 15 minutes exercises).

    Variables

    A variable is a named place that stores a value, such as total or stamps. Think of a labelled box: you can put a value in, look at it, and replace it.

    SET total TO 0
SET total TO total + 5

    After these two lines, total holds 5. The second line means “work out total + 5, then put the answer back into total”.

    Choose names that say what the value is (hours_worked, not x). Each variable holds one type of data, the types you met in Week 2: integer, float, text or Boolean.

    Sequence, selection and repetition

    Every algorithm, however large, is built from just three structures.

    1. Sequence: steps that run one after another, in order.

    2. Selection: choosing a path with IF. The condition is a Boolean test (true or false), like the logic gates in Week 2.

    IF age >= 18 THEN
    OUTPUT "Adult ticket"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Child ticket"
END IF

    3. Repetition (also called iteration or a loop): doing steps again and again.

    • A condition-controlled loop repeats while something is true:

      SET attempts TO 0
SET correct TO false
WHILE correct = false AND attempts < 3
    INPUT password
    SET attempts TO attempts + 1
    IF password = stored_password THEN
        SET correct TO true
    END IF
END WHILE

      This is how a login stops after three wrong tries.

    • A count-controlled loop repeats once for each item:

      FOR EACH price IN prices
    SET total TO total + price
END FOR

    Functions

    A function is a named set of steps that you can use again and again. It can take values in (called parameters) and give a value back with RETURN.

    FUNCTION gst(amount)
    RETURN amount * 0.1
END FUNCTION

SET tax TO gst(250)

    Here tax becomes 25. Functions keep algorithms short and tidy. You write the steps once, give them a clear name, and call them whenever you need them. You can also fix a mistake in one place.

    Basic data structures

    A data structure is a way of organising several values together.

    Structure What it is Example
    List (or array) Values in order, each with a numbered position called an index names = ["Ahmed", "Brown", "Chen"]. In this course, position 1 is "Ahmed" (many programming languages start counting at 0).
    Record One item with several named fields A customer: name, email, stamps
    Table Many records with the same fields: rows and columns A spreadsheet of customers
    Dictionary (or map) Values looked up by a key instead of a position "Olivia" → 7 stamps, "Jack" → 2 stamps

    Data scientists spend much of their time choosing and reshaping data structures, and Introduction to Programming covers Python’s versions of each.

    Checking an algorithm with a trace table

    A trace table tracks the value of each variable, step by step, as you work through an algorithm by hand. It is how you find mistakes before any code is written.

    Example: total the list of prices [4, 5, 5].

    SET total TO 0
FOR EACH price IN prices
    SET total TO total + price
END FOR
OUTPUT total
    Step price total Output
    Start – 0
    Loop 1 4 4
    Loop 2 5 9
    Loop 3 5 14
    End 14

    Choose test cases that check the tricky parts too: an empty list, a value right on a boundary (exactly 15 in the parking example), or the moment a rule changes.

    Searching: linear and binary search

    Searching is one of the most common jobs a computer does. There are two classic algorithms.

    Linear search: check each item in turn, from the start, until you find the target or reach the end.

    • It works on any list, sorted or not.
    • In a list of 1,000 items it may take up to 1,000 checks.

    Binary search: only for a sorted list.

    1. Look at the middle item. If the list has an even number of items, use the left one of the two middle items.
    2. If it is the target, stop.
    3. If the target comes before it, throw away the right half. If the target comes after it, throw away the left half.
    4. Repeat on the half that is left, until you find the target or nothing is left.

    Each check halves what is left, so binary search is very fast on large lists:

    Items in the list Most checks, linear search Most checks, binary search
    16 16 5
    1,000 1,000 10
    1,000,000 1,000,000 20

    Example: find Chen in this sorted list of 8 names, using binary search:

    Position 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
    Name Ahmed Brown Chen Davis Evans Garcia Huang Jones
    1. Positions 1 to 8. The middle is position 4 (Davis). Chen comes before Davis, so keep positions 1 to 3.
    2. The middle of 1 to 3 is position 2 (Brown). Chen comes after Brown, so keep position 3.
    3. Position 3 is Chen. Found in 3 checks. Linear search would also take 3 checks here, because Chen is near the start.

    The trade-off: binary search needs the list to be sorted first, and sorting takes work. For a list you search many times, it is worth it.

    Challenge

    Exercises

    About 15 minutes. Answers are at the end.

    1. Which structure (sequence, selection or repetition) does each describe? (a) “Repeat for every invoice.” (b) “If the invoice is overdue, send a reminder.” (c) “Open the file, then read the first line.”

    2. Complete a trace table for this algorithm with the list [3, 8, 2]:

      SET biggest TO 0
FOR EACH n IN numbers
    IF n > biggest THEN
        SET biggest TO n
    END IF
END FOR
OUTPUT biggest

    3. Write a function area(width, height) that returns the area of a rectangle, and use it to set room to the area of a 4 × 5 room.

    4. Using binary search on the 8 names above, how many checks does it take to find Huang? List the names you check.

    5. Why can’t binary search be used on an unsorted list?

      1. repetition; (b) selection; (c) sequence.

    2. Trace table:

      Step n biggest Output
      Start – 0
      Loop 1 3 3
      Loop 2 8 8
      Loop 3 2 8
      End 8

    3. For example:

      FUNCTION area(width, height)
    RETURN width * height
END FUNCTION

SET room TO area(4, 5)

      room is 20.

    4. 3 checks: Davis (position 4), then Garcia (position 6, the middle of 5 to 8), then Huang (position 7).

    5. Binary search decides which half to throw away by comparing with the middle item. That only works if everything before the middle is smaller and everything after is larger, which is true only for a sorted list.

    4.3 Down to the hardware: the Little Man Computer

    Time: about 35 minutes (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes in the simulator).

    From algorithm to machine instructions

    In Week 1 you learned that the CPU repeats the fetch-decode-execute cycle. But what exactly does it fetch? The answer is machine instructions: very small steps such as “load a number”, “add a number” or “store a number”. Each is stored in memory as a number.

    Your pseudocode in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 had big steps like FOR EACH price IN prices. A real CPU cannot do that in one go. Every big step must be broken down into many tiny machine instructions. The Concepts Bridge explains how that translation happens. In this section you will write the tiny instructions yourself.

    The Little Man Computer

    The Little Man Computer (LMC) is a simple model of a CPU, made for teaching. It works like a real computer, but it has only:

    • 100 memory locations (called mailboxes), numbered 00 to 99, each holding a three-digit number;
    • an accumulator: a single register where all the arithmetic happens;
    • a program counter: the register that holds the address of the next instruction;
    • an instruction register and an address register, which hold the instruction being worked on and the mailbox it uses;
    • an INPUT box and an OUTPUT box.

    You will use Peter Higginson’s free online LMC simulator, https://peterhigginson.co.uk/lmc/. It runs in your browser, with no account.

    The instruction set

    The LMC understands only a handful of instructions. Each one has a short name called a mnemonic. Writing programs with mnemonics is called assembly language.

    Mnemonic Machine code What it does
    INP 901 Take a number from the INPUT box and put it in the accumulator
    OUT 902 Copy the accumulator to the OUTPUT box
    STA x 3xx Store the accumulator into mailbox x
    LDA x 5xx Load the number in mailbox x into the accumulator
    ADD x 1xx Add the number in mailbox x to the accumulator
    SUB x 2xx Subtract the number in mailbox x from the accumulator
    HLT 000 Halt: stop the program
    DAT – Not an instruction: it reserves a mailbox to hold data

    (There are also three branch instructions, BRA, BRZ and BRP, which jump to another instruction. They make selection and loops possible. They are optional this week.)

    A label is a name you give to a mailbox, such as FIRST, so you do not have to work out its number. The simulator works out the numbers for you when it assembles the program, that is, turns the mnemonics into machine code.

    Reading the add program

    This program adds two numbers. Download it as add.lmc.

            INP
        STA FIRST
        INP
        ADD FIRST
        OUT
        HLT
FIRST   DAT

    Read it as a sequence:

    Line Instruction What happens
    1 INP Read the first number into the accumulator
    2 STA FIRST Store it in the mailbox labelled FIRST, so it is not lost
    3 INP Read the second number into the accumulator
    4 ADD FIRST Add the first number to it
    5 OUT Output the answer
    6 HLT Stop
    7 FIRST DAT Mailbox 06 is reserved for the first number

    When assembled, the program becomes these numbers in mailboxes 00 to 06: 901 306 901 106 902 000 000. That is the machine code. 306 means “store (3) into mailbox 06”, and 106 means “add (1) mailbox 06”.

    Compare it with pseudocode: four lines of pseudocode (INPUT a, INPUT b, SET total TO a + b, OUTPUT total) became six machine instructions, plus a mailbox. Real programs become millions of instructions.

    Running it in the simulator

    1. Open https://peterhigginson.co.uk/lmc/.
    2. Click in the Assembly Language Code box on the left and type (or paste) the add program. Use spaces to line up the columns; upper-case letters are safest.
    3. Submit and Cancel buttons appear under the code box. Click Submit. The program is assembled: the machine code appears in mailboxes 00 to 06.
    4. Click RUN. The simulator animates each fetch-decode-execute cycle. Click >> a few times to speed it up, or << to slow it down.
    5. When the message says INPUT required, click in the INPUT box, type 7 and press Enter. Do the same with 5 when asked again.
    6. Watch the accumulator, the program counter and the mailboxes change. The answer 12 appears in the OUTPUT box, and the message says the program has HALTED.
    7. To step through one instruction at a time, use STEP instead of RUN. To start again, click RESET.

    As it runs, notice the message at the bottom: FETCH CYCLE (get the instruction, add 1 to the program counter), then the execute step. This is the cycle from Week 1, made visible.

    Challenge

    Exercises

    About 10 minutes, using the simulator. Answers are at the end.

    1. Run the add program with the inputs 20 and 22. What is the output?

    2. After the program halts, which mailbox holds the first number you typed?

    3. What is the program counter’s value just after the HLT instruction is fetched, and why?

    4. What machine code would SUB FIRST become, if FIRST is mailbox 06?

    5. Predict the output of this program with the input 6, then check it in the simulator:

              INP
        STA A
        ADD A
        OUT
        HLT
A       DAT
    1. 42.
    2. Mailbox 06, the one labelled FIRST.
    3. 06. During the fetch cycle the program counter goes up by 1, ready for the next instruction, so after fetching the HLT in mailbox 05 it holds 06. (Accept 6.)
    4. 206 (2 for subtract, 06 for the mailbox).
    5. 12. It stores 6 in A, then adds A to the accumulator (which still holds 6), so it outputs 6 + 6. The program doubles any number.

    Concepts Bridge: How code becomes something the CPU can run

    Time: about 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes activity).

    Why this matters

    In Section 4.3 you wrote instructions so simple that the CPU could run them almost directly. Real software is written in languages such as Python, Java or C, which people can read. Something has to translate between the two. Knowing how this works explains:

    • why Python programs need Python installed to run, while a downloaded .exe program does not;
    • why cyber security analysts sometimes study machine code, to find out what a suspicious program really does when nobody has its source code;
    • why the same program may need a different version for Windows, macOS or a phone.

    The big idea: levels of language

    Level Example Who reads it
    High-level language Python: total = price * 2 People. It looks a little like English and maths.
    Assembly language LMC: LDA PRICE, ADD PRICE, STA TOTAL Specialists. One line per machine instruction, using mnemonics.
    Machine code 510 110 311 The CPU. Only numbers (in a real computer, binary).

    One line of a high-level language usually becomes many machine instructions. The program a person writes is called source code.

    Each kind of CPU has its own machine code. The CPU in most Windows laptops (x86) and the CPU in a phone or recent Mac (ARM) speak different “languages”. That is why software is made in separate versions.

    Two ways to translate: compilers and interpreters

    A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before it runs, and saves the result as a new file, such as an .exe.

    • It is like translating a whole book into English once, then printing it. Readers never need the translator again.
    • The finished program runs fast, and the user does not need the source code or the compiler.
    • If you change the source code, you must compile it again.
    • Examples: C, C++, Rust, Go.

    An interpreter translates and runs the program one statement at a time, every time it runs.

    • It is like a live interpreter at a meeting, translating each sentence as it is spoken.
    • It is easy to test small changes straight away, but it is usually slower, and the user needs the interpreter installed.
    • Examples: Python, JavaScript (in your web browser), PHP.

    Some languages use a mix. Java and C#, for example, compile to an in-between form that a “virtual machine” then runs. You do not need the details for this course.

    An assembler is the simplest translator of all: it turns assembly language into machine code, one line to one instruction. When you clicked Submit in the LMC simulator, an assembler turned STA FIRST into 306.

    Worked example

    This Python line:

    total = price + price

    could become these LMC instructions:

            LDA PRICE      load price into the accumulator
        ADD PRICE      add price again
        STA TOTAL      store the result in total

    which the assembler turns into machine code, if PRICE is mailbox 10 and TOTAL is mailbox 11:

    510 110 311

    One readable line became three instructions, then three numbers.

    Challenge

    Activity (15 minutes)

    1. Sort these into compiled or interpreted, using the examples above: (a) a Python script (.py file); (b) a game you download as an .exe; (c) JavaScript on a website.
    2. In three or four sentences, explain to a friend why you need Python installed to run a .py file, but you can run most .exe programs straight away.
    3. Write LMC instructions for the Python line total = price - discount. Use the labels PRICE, DISCOUNT and TOTAL. Then give the machine code, if PRICE is mailbox 10, DISCOUNT is 11 and TOTAL is 12.
      1. interpreted; (b) compiled; (c) interpreted.

    2. For example: “A .py file is source code. It has to be translated each time it runs, and the program that does that translating, the Python interpreter, must be on your computer. An .exe was compiled before it was given to you. It is already machine code that your CPU can run, so no translator is needed.”

    3. Assembly and machine code:

              LDA PRICE
        SUB DISCOUNT
        STA TOTAL

      The machine code is 510 211 312.

    Practice task: Algorithm design

    Callout

    Files for this task

    Download single files here, or every course file at once in the course files zip. Worksheets download as plain text (.txt): open one in any text editor, and save your copy with the name the task gives.

    • algorithm_design_worksheet.txt

    Time: about 2 hours. This is your portfolio item for Week 4. Your tutor marks it at the end of the week.

    Goal

    Design, draw and test an algorithm for a real business rule. Then compare two search algorithms, and change a machine-level program.

    Work in the worksheet. Save your copy as algorithm_design.md. Any text editor works, or you can copy it into Word or Google Docs and save it as a PDF.

    The problem: the Bean There café loyalty card

    The Bean There café (an invented business) wants an algorithm for its loyalty card. The rules are:

    • A coffee costs $5.00. On Tuesdays it costs $4.00.
    • Each coffee the customer pays for earns one stamp.
    • When the card already has 9 stamps, the next coffee is free, and the card goes back to 0 stamps. A free coffee does not earn a stamp.
    • The algorithm is given the customer’s starting number of stamps and a list of the days they buy a coffee, one coffee per day in the list.
    • It must output a message for each free coffee, then the total amount paid and the number of stamps left on the card.

    Part 1: pseudocode (about 30 minutes)

    1. Decompose the problem. List three or four smaller parts.
    2. Write the algorithm in pseudocode, using the keywords from Section 4.1. It must use:
      • at least two variables (for example stamps and total);
      • a loop over the list of days;
      • an IF decision;
      • a function price_for(day) that returns the price for a given day.

    Part 2: flowchart (about 25 minutes)

    Draw the same algorithm as a flowchart in diagrams.net (https://app.diagrams.net/), or by hand.

    • Use the correct shapes: terminator, input/output, process and decision.
    • Label the Yes and No arrows from each decision.
    • Show the loop with an arrow that goes back up.

    Export it as a PNG (File > Export as > PNG) or photograph it, and add it to the worksheet. You may show the price_for function as a single process box, “work out price for day”.

    Part 3: trace tables (about 25 minutes)

    Test your pseudocode by hand with the two test cases below. Fill in a trace table for each, showing day, price, stamps, total and any output on every pass of the loop.

    Test Starting stamps Days
    1 0 Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday
    2 7 Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday

    If your trace shows a result that breaks the café’s rules, fix your pseudocode and trace it again. Say what you changed.

    Part 4: linear search compared with binary search (about 15 minutes)

    Here is a sorted list of 16 customer surnames:

    Position 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
    Name Ahmed Brown Chen Davis Evans Garcia Huang Jones
    Position 9 10 11 12 13 14 15 16
    Name Kelly Lee Martin Nguyen Patel Smith Taylor Wilson

    For Patel and for Brown:

    1. Count the checks that linear search takes.
    2. Use binary search, following the steps in Section 4.2. Remember: with an even number of items, the middle is the left one of the two middle items. List each name you check, and count the checks.
    3. In two or three sentences: which search was faster for each name, and why is binary search still the better choice for a long, sorted list?

    Part 5: change a Little Man Computer program (about 15 minutes)

    1. Open the add program in the LMC simulator (https://peterhigginson.co.uk/lmc/), as in Section 4.3, and run it once with 7 and 5 to check it outputs 12.
    2. Change it so it subtracts the second number from the first. Hint: SUB takes away a mailbox’s value from the accumulator, so the first number must be in the accumulator and the second number in a mailbox. You will need a second DAT mailbox.
    3. Run your program with 9 and 4 (expected output 5) and with 3 and 9 (expected output −6).
    4. Paste your program into the worksheet, and take one screenshot after the 3 and 9 run, showing the output.

    Part 6: reflection (about 10 minutes, plus tidying)

    Write 100 to 150 words:

    1. Did your trace tables find a mistake? If so, what was it? If not, how did you check carefully?
    2. What surprised you about how many machine instructions a simple task needs?
    3. How might you use algorithm design (decomposition, pseudocode, trace tables) in cyber security or data science?

    Check your work

    How it is marked

    Your tutor marks each criterion as meets, partly or not yet:

    Criterion What the tutor looks for
    Accurate The algorithm follows the rules. The traces, search counts and LMC output are correct.
    Complete Every item on the checklist is done.
    Evidence The trace tables, flowchart image and LMC screenshot are included.
    Explanation The search comparison and the reflection are in your own words.

    Key Points

    • Each week has five blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge, Build and Quiz.
    • An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step solution.
    • Pseudocode and flowcharts let you plan before you code.
    • Every program is built from sequence, selection and repetition.
    • Binary search is much faster, but only works on sorted data.
    • Each instruction is fetched, decoded and executed in turn.
    • Real programs are made of many simple instructions like these.
    • Compilers and interpreters translate code into instructions the CPU can run.
    • Test an algorithm by hand with a trace table before you trust it.

    5.1 Networks and the internet

    Time: about 40 minutes (30 minutes reading, 10 minutes exercises).

    What a network is

    A network is two or more devices connected so they can share data.

    Type What it covers Example
    LAN (local area network) One home, office or building The office Wi-Fi and the printers on it
    WAN (wide area network) A large area, joining LANs together A company linking its Perth and Sydney offices
    The internet A worldwide network of networks Billions of devices, joined by agreed rules

    The internet is not owned by one company. It works because every connected network follows the same protocols: agreed rules for how data is formatted and sent.

    Network devices

    Device What it does
    Switch Connects devices inside a LAN, and sends each piece of data only to the device it is meant for
    Router Connects different networks together (for example your LAN to the internet), and chooses the path for data to travel
    Wireless access point Lets devices join the LAN by Wi-Fi
    Modem / NBN connection box Connects your network to your internet service provider (ISP)
    Firewall Checks traffic coming in and going out, and blocks what is not allowed

    At home, one small box usually does the jobs of the router, switch, access point and firewall together.

    Packets

    Data does not travel across a network in one piece. It is split into small chunks called packets. Each packet carries: - a piece of the data - the source address (where it came from) - the destination address (where it is going) - a number, so the pieces can be put back in order

    Routers pass each packet along, hop by hop, towards its destination. Different packets may take different routes. The receiving computer puts them back together. This is called packet switching. If a route is broken, packets simply go another way, which makes the internet very resilient.

    IP addresses

    Every device on a network needs an address, called its IP address (Internet Protocol address).

    IPv4 addresses look like 192.168.1.25: four numbers separated by dots. Each number is one byte, so it is between 0 and 255 (remember Week 2). That gives about 4.3 billion possible addresses, which is not enough for today’s devices.

    IPv6 addresses are much longer and written in hex, for example 2403:4800:9003:2::794f:7f41. There are enough IPv6 addresses for every device we could ever build.

    Public and private addresses

    • A public IP address is unique on the whole internet. Your home or office usually has one public address, given by the ISP.
    • A private IP address is used only inside a LAN, and the same private address can be reused in millions of homes. Private IPv4 addresses start with:
      • 10.
      • 172.16. to 172.31.
      • 192.168.

    The router swaps between the private and public addresses as data goes in and out.

    Callout

    Privacy: your public IP address can show roughly where you are. Do not post it, or put it in your course work.

    Subnets. A large network is often divided into smaller parts called subnets: for example, one for staff computers and one for guest Wi-Fi. That keeps them apart, and it is a common security control. In an address such as 192.168.1.25/24, the /24 means the first 24 bits (the first three numbers, 192.168.1) identify the subnet, and the last number identifies the device. You do not need to calculate subnets in this course.

    DNS: names for addresses

    People remember names like abc.net.au. Computers need IP addresses. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the internet’s address book: it turns a domain name into an IP address. This is called resolving the name.

    DNS stores several kinds of record:

    Record What it holds Example use
    A An IPv4 address for the name Where to find the website
    AAAA An IPv6 address for the name The same, for IPv6
    MX The mail servers that accept email for the domain Where to deliver email sent to someone@abc.net.au
    CNAME Another name this name points to (an alias) www.abc.net.au points to a content delivery network

    Attackers sometimes try to tamper with DNS, so that a real name leads to a fake site. That is one reason DNS matters to cyber security.

    Ports and protocols

    An IP address gets data to the right device. A port number gets it to the right program on that device, as a flat number gets mail to the right door in an apartment block.

    Port Protocol What it is for
    22 SSH Logging in to another computer securely, using the command line
    25 SMTP Sending email between mail servers
    53 DNS Looking up names
    80 HTTP Web pages, not encrypted
    443 HTTPS Web pages, encrypted

    Security analysts check which ports are open on a device. Every open port is a door that an attacker might try.

    TCP and UDP

    Two protocols carry most data across the internet.

    TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
    How it works Sets up a connection first, numbers every packet, and resends any that go missing Just sends the packets, with no checking
    Strength Reliable: everything arrives, in order Fast, with low delay
    Used for Web pages, email, file downloads Video calls, online games, live streaming, most DNS lookups

    A dropped frame in a video call does not matter much. A missing piece of a bank transfer does. That is why each kind of app uses a different protocol.

    The layer model

    Network jobs are split into layers. Each layer does one job and relies on the layer below. The TCP/IP model has four:

    TCP/IP layer Job Examples OSI layers (another model you will meet later)
    Application What the user’s program wants to send HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SMTP 7 Application, 6 Presentation, 5 Session
    Transport Delivery between programs, using ports TCP, UDP 4 Transport
    Internet Addressing and routing between networks IP 3 Network
    Link Moving data across one physical link Ethernet cable, Wi-Fi 2 Data link, 1 Physical

    The seven-layer OSI model is often used in networking and security courses. You only need to know that it exists and lines up with the four TCP/IP layers like this.

    Challenge

    Exercises

    About 10 minutes. Answers are at the end.

    1. LAN, WAN or the internet? (a) the Wi-Fi in a café; (b) a bank linking all its branches; (c) watching a video from an overseas website.
    2. Which device: (a) joins your home network to the internet and chooses paths; (b) connects the computers inside an office?
    3. Why can’t 192.168.1.300 be a valid IPv4 address?
    4. Public or private: (a) 10.0.0.5; (b) 121.79.127.65; (c) 192.168.0.10?
    5. Which DNS record tells the world where to deliver email for a domain?
    6. Would you use TCP or UDP for (a) downloading a PDF; (b) a live video call? Why?
      1. LAN; (b) WAN; (c) the internet.
      1. a router; (b) a switch.
    3. Each part is one byte, so it must be from 0 to 255. 300 is too big.
      1. private; (b) public; (c) private.
    5. The MX record.
      1. TCP, because the file must arrive complete and in order; (b) UDP, because speed matters more than an occasional lost packet.

    5.2 The web, HTTP and HTTPS

    Time: about 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes trying the tools).

    The internet and the web are different

    The internet is the network: the cables, routers and protocols that move packets. The World Wide Web is one service that runs on the internet: pages linked together and shown in a browser. Email, video calls and online games also use the internet, but they are not the web.

    The parts of a web address

    A web address is called a URL (uniform resource locator).

    https://www.abc.net.au/news/science?page=2
    Part Example Meaning
    Scheme https The protocol to use
    Host (domain name) www.abc.net.au The server to contact; DNS turns it into an IP address
    Path /news/science Which page or file on that server
    Query ?page=2 Extra information sent to the server

    Read the domain carefully. In abc.net.au.login-check.com, the real domain is login-check.com. Everything before it is just a label that its owner chose. Phishing links often use this trick (Section 5.3).

    Requests and responses

    The web uses HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol). Your browser sends a request, and the server sends back a response.

    A request has a method:

    • GET asks for something, such as a page or an image.
    • POST sends something, such as a form you filled in.

    Every response starts with a status code:

    Code Meaning When you see it
    200 OK It worked Almost every normal page and image
    301 Moved permanently Go to a different address instead http://abc.net.au redirects to https://www.abc.net.au
    403 Forbidden You are not allowed A page you have no permission for
    404 Not found It does not exist A mistyped address
    500 Internal server error Something broke on the server A fault in the website itself

    A rule of thumb: codes in the 200s mean success, 300s mean redirect, 400s mean a problem with the request, and 500s mean a problem on the server.

    One web page is rarely one request. The browser first gets the HTML page, then makes dozens of further requests for images, styles, scripts and fonts, often from other servers.

    HTTPS and certificates

    Plain HTTP is sent as readable text. Anyone on the path, such as someone on the same public Wi-Fi, could read or change it.

    HTTPS is HTTP sent inside an encrypted connection, using a protocol called TLS. It gives three protections:

    1. Confidentiality: the data is encrypted, so people on the path cannot read it.
    2. Integrity: if anyone changes the data on the way, it is detected.
    3. Authentication: the server proves who it is with a certificate.

    A certificate is a digital document that says “this public key belongs to www.abc.net.au”. It is signed by a trusted certificate authority (CA), and it has an expiry date. Your browser checks the certificate every time. If something is wrong, it shows a full-page warning. Do not click past these warnings.

    Callout

    The padlock means “encrypted”, not “safe”. Scammers can get certificates for their own fake sites too. A padlock on abc-net-au-login.com only proves you have a private, encrypted line to a scammer. Always check the domain name.

    Try it: your browser’s developer tools

    Every modern browser has developer tools that show each request a page makes. These steps are for Chrome or Edge; Firefox and Safari are similar.

    1. Open a new tab and go to https://www.abc.net.au.
    2. Press F12, or Ctrl + Shift + I (Windows) or Cmd + Option + I (Mac). Choose the Network tab.
    3. Press F5 (or Cmd + R) to reload the page, so the requests are recorded.
    4. Each row is one request. Look at the Name, Status, Type and Size columns. The first row (type document) is the page itself.
    5. Click a row, then Headers, to see its Request URL, Request Method and Status Code.
    6. Now go to https://www.abc.net.au/this-page-does-not-exist and look at the first row’s status. It should be 404.

    If developer tools are blocked on your work laptop, use a home or library computer. If you have none, see the alternative in the practice task.

    View a certificate:

    1. Click the icon to the left of the address (a padlock or a “tune” icon).
    2. Choose Connection is secure.
    3. Choose Certificate is valid.
    4. Note Issued to, Issued by and the Valid to (expiry) date.

    Try it: look up DNS records

    1. Go to Google Admin Toolbox Dig: https://toolbox.googleapps.com/apps/dig/. It runs in your browser, with no account.
    2. Type abc.net.au in the box, and choose the record type A. The answer lists one or more IPv4 addresses.
    3. Choose MX. The answer lists the mail servers. The number in front of each (for example 10) is its priority: lower numbers are tried first.
    4. Try www.abc.net.au with CNAME. It points to another name, which belongs to the network that delivers the site’s content.

    DNS records change over time, so your answers may not match a classmate’s exactly.

    Challenge

    Exercises

    About 5 minutes. Answers are at the end.

    1. In https://shop.example.com.au/cart?item=42, what are the host, the path and the query?
    2. What do these status codes mean: (a) 404; (b) 301; (c) 500?
    3. A site shows a padlock. Does that prove the site is honest? Explain.
    4. In the URL https://mygov.au.secure-login.net/signin, what is the real domain?
    1. Host: shop.example.com.au. Path: /cart. Query: ?item=42.
      1. not found; (b) moved permanently (a redirect); (c) an error on the server.
    3. No. It proves the connection is encrypted and the certificate matches the name in the address bar. A scammer can get a certificate for their own domain.
    4. secure-login.net. It is not the real myGov domain.

    5.3 Online safety and cyber security basics

    Time: about 45 minutes (30 minutes reading, 5 minutes in CyberChef, 10 minutes exercises).

    The CIA triad

    Cyber security protects three things about information, known as the CIA triad:

    Goal Meaning What breaks it
    Confidentiality Only the right people can see the information A stolen password lets a stranger read your email
    Integrity The information is accurate and has not been changed without permission An attacker changes the bank account number on an invoice
    Availability The information and systems work when needed Ransomware locks every file, so the business cannot trade

    Almost every security control you will study protects one or more of these.

    Common threats

    Threat What it is
    Malware Any harmful software. The general term for the threats below.
    Virus Malware that attaches to files and spreads when they are opened
    Worm Malware that spreads across a network by itself
    Trojan Malware disguised as something useful, such as a “free” program
    Spyware Malware that secretly watches you, for example recording what you type
    Ransomware Malware that encrypts your files and demands payment to unlock them
    Phishing Fake messages (email, text or call) that trick you into clicking, paying or giving away details. Texts are sometimes called smishing.
    Social engineering Manipulating people rather than computers, for example pretending to be IT support
    Scams Fraud that tricks people out of money: fake invoices, fake investments, fake parcels

    Most successful attacks start with a person being tricked, not with clever code. That is why awareness matters as much as technology.

    Spotting phishing

    Common clues:

    1. Urgency or fear: “Your account will be closed in 24 hours.”
    2. A sender address that is slightly wrong, such as support@rnygov.com (r-n, not m) or a free email address for a “bank”.
    3. Links that go somewhere else. Hover over a link (or press and hold on a phone) to see the real address, then read the domain as you learned in Section 5.2.
    4. Requests for passwords, codes or payment. Real organisations do not ask for your password or your multi-factor code.
    5. Unexpected attachments, especially archives or files whose real type does not match their name (remember invoice.pdf in Week 2).
    6. Changed bank details on an invoice. Always confirm with a phone number you already have, not one in the email.
    7. Generic greetings and odd wording, although modern scams are often well written, so do not rely on spelling mistakes.

    Passwords and multi-factor authentication

    Authentication means proving who you are. It can use: - something you know (a password or PIN) - something you have (a phone, a security key) - something you are (a fingerprint or your face)

    Good passwords:

    • Long beats complicated. A passphrase of four or more random words (for example crystal onion clay pretzel) is much harder to guess than P@ssw0rd1, and easier to remember.
    • Unique for every account. When one website is breached, attackers try the stolen email and password on many other sites. This is called credential stuffing.
    • Use a password manager to create and remember unique passwords. You then only need to remember one strong passphrase.

    Multi-factor authentication (MFA) asks for a second kind of proof, such as a code from an app, as well as your password. Even if your password is stolen, the attacker cannot log in without the second factor. Turn it on for email, banking and social media first.

    Encoding, encryption and hashing

    These three are often confused. They all change how data looks, but for different reasons:

    Encoding Encryption Hashing
    Purpose Store or send data in a different format Keep data secret Check data has not changed, or store passwords safely
    Can it be reversed? Yes, by anyone, with no key Yes, but only with the key No. It is one-way.
    Example ASCII, hex, Base64 HTTPS, an encrypted laptop drive A SHA-256 fingerprint of a file; how websites store passwords

    A hash is a fixed-length “fingerprint” of any data. Change one letter of the input and the hash changes completely.

    Websites should store a hash of your password, never the password itself. When you log in, they hash what you typed and compare the two hashes.

    Try it (5 minutes). CyberChef (https://gchq.github.io/CyberChef/) is a free tool made by the UK’s signals intelligence agency, GCHQ. It runs entirely in your browser: what you type is not sent anywhere. Do not type real passwords into it anyway.

    1. Type ADCI in the Input box.
    2. From the Operations list on the left, drag To Base64 into the Recipe column. The output is QURDSQ==. This is encoding. Drag in From Base64 below it, and you get ADCI back.
    3. Clear the recipe (the bin icon), and drag in SHA2. Set its Size to 256. The output is a 64-character hash starting 37ca1ddb.
    4. Change the input to ADCJ, which differs by one letter. The hash changes completely: it now starts afb60119. There is no “From SHA2” operation, because hashing cannot be reversed.

    In Introduction to Programming, Part 2 Week 3, you will hash data in Python.

    Everyday protections

    • Install updates promptly, for the operating system, browser and apps (Week 3).
    • Back up important files, and keep at least one copy that ransomware cannot reach: a drive you disconnect after each backup, or a cloud backup that keeps earlier versions. (A folder that simply syncs to the cloud can be encrypted along with your files.)
    • Public Wi-Fi: HTTPS protects your web traffic, but avoid banking on unknown networks if you can, and never ignore certificate warnings. Your phone’s hotspot is safer.
    • Lock your screen when you walk away, and use a PIN or biometric on your phone.
    • Think before you share: details you post can be used to guess passwords or make a scam convincing.

    Reporting

    In Australia:

    • Report cybercrime to the Australian Cyber Security Centre through ReportCyber: https://www.cyber.gov.au/report-and-recover/report
    • Report scams to Scamwatch: https://www.scamwatch.gov.au/
    • At work, report suspicious messages to your IT or security team straight away. Reporting quickly, even after you clicked, limits the damage.
    Challenge

    Exercises

    About 10 minutes. Answers are at the end.

    1. Which part of the CIA triad is harmed? (a) A website is knocked offline. (b) Customer records are leaked online. (c) An attacker changes the grades in a school system.
    2. Name the threat: (a) a free game that secretly installs a keylogger; (b) malware that locks files and demands payment; (c) a caller pretending to be from IT asking for your password.
    3. An email from “Australia Post” says a parcel is held, and gives a link to auspost.parcel-redelivery.info. List two clues that it is phishing.
    4. Why is crystal onion clay pretzel a better password than Tr0ub4dor&3?
    5. Encoding, encryption or hashing? (a) a laptop drive that needs a key to read; (b) a fingerprint used to check a downloaded file has not been changed; (c) turning text into Base64 to send it in an email.
      1. availability; (b) confidentiality; (c) integrity.
      1. a trojan (carrying spyware); (b) ransomware; (c) social engineering.
    3. Any two: the real domain is parcel-redelivery.info, not auspost.com.au; it creates urgency about a parcel; it was unexpected; it asks you to click a link.
    4. It is longer, so there are far more possible combinations to guess, and it is easier to remember. Swapping letters for numbers and symbols adds little, because attackers’ tools already try those swaps.
      1. encryption; (b) hashing; (c) encoding.

    Concepts Bridge: What happens when you type a web address

    Time: about 30 minutes (15 minutes reading, 15 minutes activity).

    Why this matters

    “What happens when you type a web address and press Enter?” is a classic question in IT and cyber security job interviews, because a good answer touches almost every layer of computing. It is also the map an analyst uses to work out where something went wrong: a DNS problem, a network problem, a certificate problem or a server problem.

    The big idea: eight steps

    You type https://www.abc.net.au into your browser and press Enter.

    Step What happens Week and section
    1. Input The keyboard sends the keystrokes; the browser reads the URL and sees the scheme https and the host www.abc.net.au. Week 1 (IPOS), Section 5.2
    2. DNS lookup The browser needs an IP address. It checks its own memory (cache) first, then asks a DNS server (often your router or ISP). www.abc.net.au turns out to be an alias (CNAME) for a content delivery network, which finally gives an A record: an IP address. Section 5.1
    3. Find the route Your computer sees that the address is not on your LAN, so it sends the packets to your router, which passes them to your ISP, and from router to router across the internet. Section 5.1
    4. TCP connection The browser opens a TCP connection to port 443 on that server, so that nothing will be lost on the way. Section 5.1
    5. TLS handshake The server sends its certificate. The browser checks that it was signed by a trusted certificate authority, matches www.abc.net.au and has not expired. They agree on encryption keys. From now on everything is encrypted. Section 5.2
    6. HTTP request The browser sends GET / inside the encrypted connection. Section 5.2
    7. HTTP response The server replies with status 200 and the HTML of the page. Section 5.2
    8. Render (output) The browser reads the HTML, then makes dozens more requests (steps 2 to 7 again) for images, styles and scripts, and draws the page on the screen. Week 1 (output)

    All of this usually happens in under a second.

    Where things go wrong

    Symptom Most likely step
    “This site can’t be reached: server IP address could not be found” 2: DNS
    The page spins and times out; other sites fail too 3: the network or route
    A full-page “Your connection is not private” warning 5: the certificate (expired, wrong name, or someone is intercepting)
    “404 Not Found” 7: the server is reachable but has no such page
    “500 Internal Server Error” 7: a fault on the server
    Challenge

    Activity (15 minutes)

    1. Without looking at the table above, write the eight steps in your own words, in order. Then check your list against the table.
    2. For each problem below, say which step most likely failed and what you would check first:
        1. A colleague can open every site except one, which gives “server IP address could not be found”.
      • (b) On hotel Wi-Fi, every site shows “Your connection is not private”.
      • (c) A link in an old email gives “404 Not Found”.
    3. In two or three sentences: at which step does HTTPS protect you on public Wi-Fi, and what does it not protect you from?
    1. Any wording that keeps the order is fine: input; DNS lookup; route through the router; TCP connection; TLS handshake and certificate check; HTTP request; HTTP response; display the page and fetch the rest of its parts.
    2. Suggested answers:
        1. Step 2, DNS. Check that the name is spelled correctly, then look it up in a DNS tool to see whether it resolves.
      • (b) Step 5, certificates. The hotel network may be intercepting connections, often a login page or, in a worse case, an attack. Do not click past the warning; use your phone’s hotspot instead.
      • (c) Step 7. The server works, but the page has moved or been deleted. Search the site for it.
    3. From step 5 onwards, everything is encrypted, so others on the Wi-Fi cannot read or change the pages and passwords you send. HTTPS does not protect you from a fake website with its own valid certificate (phishing), from malware already on your device, or from someone seeing which site you visited.

    Practice task: Network investigation and online safety checklist

    Callout

    Files for this task

    Download single files here, or every course file at once in the course files zip. Worksheets download as plain text (.txt): open one in any text editor, and save your copy with the name the task gives.

    • network_investigation_worksheet.txt

    Time: about 2 hours. This is your portfolio item for Week 5. Your tutor marks it at the end of the week.

    Goal

    Investigate how two real websites are found, reached and secured. Then turn what you learned about online safety into practical advice for a new staff member.

    Work in the worksheet. Save your copy as network_investigation.md. Any text editor works, or you can copy it into Word or Google Docs and save it as a PDF.

    The two websites (both public Australian organisations):

    • Site A: ABC, domain abc.net.au, website https://www.abc.net.au
    • Site B: CSIRO, domain csiro.au, website https://www.csiro.au
    Callout

    Privacy. Do not record your own public IP address, or anything from your own email or accounts. Everything you need comes from the two public websites.

    DNS records and certificates change from time to time, so your values may differ from a classmate’s. That is fine, as long as you explain what each one means.

    Part 1: DNS records (about 20 minutes)

    Use Google Admin Toolbox Dig (https://toolbox.googleapps.com/apps/dig/), as in Section 5.2.

    For each domain (abc.net.au and csiro.au):

    1. Look up the A record and record the IP address or addresses.
    2. Look up the MX record and record the mail servers and their priority numbers.
    3. Say whether the IP address is public or private, and how you know.

    Then, in two or three sentences: what would go wrong for each organisation if its MX records were deleted? What if its A record pointed to the wrong address?

    Part 2: requests and status codes (about 20 minutes)

    Use your browser’s developer tools, Network tab, as in Section 5.2.

    1. Open https://www.abc.net.au with the Network tab open, and reload. Record three requests: the main page (type document), one image and one script. For each, record the method, status code, type and size.
    2. Look at the total number of requests at the bottom of the Network tab. Record it, and explain in one sentence why one page needs so many.
    3. Visit https://www.csiro.au/this-page-does-not-exist and record the status code of the main request.
    4. Visit http://abc.net.au (note: http, without www). Record the status code of the first request and the address it sends you to. Explain what happened and why the site does this.

    If developer tools are blocked on your computer: for steps 3 and 4, enter the addresses into httpstatus.io (https://httpstatus.io/), which shows each status code and redirect. For steps 1 and 2, write “developer tools blocked” and describe what you would expect to see. Your tutor will not mark you down for this.

    Part 3: certificates (about 10 minutes)

    For each website (https://www.abc.net.au and https://www.csiro.au), open the certificate viewer as in Section 5.2 and record:

    • Issued to (the common name);
    • Issued by (the certificate authority);
    • Valid to (the expiry date).

    Then answer: if the certificate’s name did not match the address bar, what would the browser do, and why?

    Part 4: the path of a request (about 20 minutes)

    Draw a diagram (in diagrams.net, as in Week 4, or by hand) showing what happens when you open https://www.csiro.au. Include and label:

    • your device, your router, the internet (as a cloud), a DNS server and the CSIRO web server;
    • the DNS lookup (question and answer);
    • the HTTPS request on port 443 using TCP, and the response with a status code;
    • where the connection is encrypted.

    Use the Concepts Bridge to help. Add the image to the worksheet.

    Part 5: phishing quiz (about 15 minutes)

    1. Take Google’s Phishing Quiz (https://phishingquiz.withgoogle.com/). It uses made-up example emails. Click Take the quiz. When it asks for a name and email address, it only uses them to fill in the pretend emails, so type a made-up name and address, not your own.
    2. Record your score.
    3. Describe two clues you learned to spot, and give an example of each from the quiz.

    Part 6: online safety checklist (about 20 minutes)

    Harbour Street Physio, the office from Week 3, has a new receptionist starting on Monday. Write a ten-point online safety checklist for them. Each point must be:

    • an action they can actually do, for example “Turn on multi-factor authentication for your work email on day one”, not “Be careful online”;
    • one line, with a short reason in brackets.

    Cover at least: passwords or passphrases, MFA, phishing, updates, public Wi-Fi, locking the screen, and how and where to report a suspicious message.

    Part 7: reflection (about 15 minutes, including tidying)

    Write 100 to 150 words:

    1. What surprised you most about what happens behind one web page?
    2. Which part of the CIA triad does HTTPS protect, and which part does a backup protect?
    3. How could DNS records, status codes or certificates help a cyber security analyst or a data analyst at work?

    Check your work

    How it is marked

    Your tutor marks each criterion as meets, partly or not yet:

    Criterion What the tutor looks for
    Accurate The records, status codes and certificate details are read and explained correctly. The diagram is in the right order.
    Complete Every item on the checklist is done.
    Evidence The recorded values and the diagram show the tools were used.
    Explanation The explanations, the checklist and the reflection are in your own words and practical.

    Key Points

    • Each week has five blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge, Build and Quiz.
    • Data travels in packets, passed from router to router.
    • DNS turns names into IP addresses.
    • HTTPS encrypts the connection; a padlock does not mean a site is honest.
    • Status codes tell you what happened to each request.
    • Most attacks start with a person being tricked.
    • Long unique passphrases and MFA stop most account takeovers.
    • DNS comes first; HTTPS encryption starts with the TLS handshake.
    • DNS, status codes and certificates are evidence you can check yourself.

    Content from Week 6: Data, the cloud, ethics and society

    Last updated on 2026-11-23 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What will I learn in Week 6, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    • What kinds of data are there, and how should they be looked after?
    • What is the cloud, and what are its benefits and risks?
    • What protects people’s data in Australia?
    • How does computing affect society?
    • Who collects data about me in an ordinary day, and what rules apply?
    • Can I bring the whole course together to advise a real-world business?

    Objectives

    • Plan your study time for the week using the time plan.
    • Sort data into structured, semi-structured and unstructured.
    • Describe the data lifecycle and data quality.
    • Explain IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, and public, private and hybrid cloud.
    • Explain data sovereignty and shared responsibility.
    • Explain digital footprints, the Privacy Act and the Australian Privacy Principles.
    • Describe the Essential Eight.
    • Discuss bias in AI and the digital divide.
    • Trace a day’s digital footprint and the organisations that collect it.
    • Carry out an IT and data health check and make prioritised recommendations.

    Week 6 overview

    Theme: what data is and how it is looked after, where it lives in the cloud, the laws and ethics that protect people, and how computing changes society. The week ends with a capstone that uses everything from Weeks 1 to 6.

    What you will be able to do this week

    • Explain the difference between data and information, and sort data into structured, semi-structured and unstructured.
    • Describe the data lifecycle and what makes data good quality.
    • Explain IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, the public, private and hybrid cloud, and why it matters where data is stored.
    • Explain digital footprints and the basics of Australian privacy law: the Privacy Act 1988, the Australian Privacy Principles and the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme.
    • Discuss how computing affects work, education and society, including AI, the digital divide and the environment.
    • Carry out a simple IT and data health check for a small business, and make plain-English recommendations.
